RNG-001.name: “True randomness” becomes a regulatory threshold called “acceptable randomness.”

RNG-002.name: A fair game requires a second operation after randomness: random numbers must be mapped into outcomes.

RNG-003.name: The RNG seed and the game’s return-to-player percentage belong to different mechanisms.

CASINO-ARCH-001.name: An online casino decomposes into components that each transform a different kind of state.

PLATFORM-001.name: A new interface channel can change while the game engine remains the same.

TEST-001.name: Simulation testing does not test “the game” at once; it tests whether one statistical consequence falls inside an acceptable range.

KANEVA-DIM-001.name: Kaneva treated 2D and 3D as alternate interfaces onto one social world rather than as separate destinations.

KANEVA-MEDIA-001.name: Kaneva did not merely embed YouTube; it converted a web media object into an object located inside a room.

KANEVA-BOUNDARY-001.name: Kaneva's world was designed around ingress: the world remained alive by admitting things that were not produced inside it.

KANEVA-HOUSE-001.name: In Kaneva, the virtual house begins to look less like simulated shelter than a spatial operating system for media and identity.

KANEVA-WORLD-001.name: Kaneva suggests that “entering the world” and “accessing the world” are different operations.

HUBS-URL-001.name: Mozilla Hubs made the URL itself into a door to a 3D world.

HUBS-MEDIA-002.name: In Hubs, pasting a URL could manufacture a manipulable object.

HUBS-DEATH-003.name: Mozilla could close Hubs without making the Hubs code cease to exist.

METAVERSE-DIM-004.name: The metaverse may be representation-independent: 2D and 3D can be clients of the same world.

ROBLOX-LAW-005.name: Roblox compiles jurisdiction, age, and platform policy into runtime variables.

ROBLOX-RANDOM-006.name: Roblox does not regulate “randomness” uniformly: paid randomness can be conditional while advertising rewards must be predetermined.

MINECRAFT-MONEY-007.name: Minecraft protects the boundary of a server by forbidding its virtual currency from crossing it.

LOOTBOX-BORDER-008.name: For UK gambling law, the border between game and world can determine whether a loot box counts as gambling.

LOOTBOX-EVIDENCE-009.name: The central loot-box evidence problem may be that the platform possesses the experiment while researchers possess only observations.

XSOLLA-EXOSKELETON-010.name: Xsolla's Web Shop lets the purchase leave the game while the purchased object stays inside it.

XSOLLA-PORTAL-011.name: Xsolla Metasites translates the hyperlink graph into a portal graph.

XSOLLA-ROBLOX-012.name: The hidden boundary of Roblox becomes visible on the credit-card statement: “Xsolla*Roblox.”

XSOLLA-MINECRAFT-013.name: A Minecraft server can acquire a second body on the web: server in 3D, commercial identity in 2D.

GAMBLING-TOPOLOGY-014.name: The casino is not the building: gambling is a topology of value, chance, and payout that can wear any architecture.

SECOND-LIFE-JURISDICTION-015.name: Second Life turns legal jurisdiction into literal geography: some avatars are not permitted to enter the region.

SECOND-LIFE-NOVELTY-016.name: A worthless virtual object can legalize a chance mechanic by failing to become money.

ROBLOX-MARBLE-017.name: Roblox's marble fountain turns a randomized transaction into a tiny piece of world physics.

ROBLOX-CASHOUT-018.name: Roblox's value membrane is asymmetric: player money can enter a random-item economy while creator earnings can leave as dollars.

XSOLLA-RANDOM-FLAG-019.name: Xsolla turns gambling-adjacentness into catalog metadata: “Mark as paid randomized reward.”

XSOLLA-CHANCE-API-020.name: The treasure chest disappears completely in Xsolla's API: “open loot box” is a remote state mutation with three identifiers.

MINECRAFT-GAMBLING-021.name: Minecraft bans “gambling” as an all-ages world-content failure while separately engineering currencies so they cannot escape the server.

WORLD-MEMBRANE-022.name: The boundary of the virtual world is part of the gambling machine.
